summary: The checker's negative arms are real and mostly well pinned, but two of them can report SUCCESS while having examined nothing or the wrong thing, both measured. (1) checkChain returns an empty list -- indistinguishable from clean -- for an absent chain, an empty chain, or a prefix that lists nothing, and the only signal that pointed at that (crossEpochOffsetsChecked()) was deleted this commit with nothing observable put back. (2) checkLink and the upTo fold take the LAST Seal in the predecessor, where the protocol's barrier is the FIRST -- so a chain with a post-seal zombie delta, a shape production's own ChainReplay.chainEnd can create, gets its successor declared clean while it inherits the fenced writer's offsets, which is exactly the masking offsetsBEYONDThePredecessorsSEALAreNOTInherited's comment says must never happen. Plus the baselines/review.txt entry states 'recorded as M4.21' and M4.21 exists nowhere in the tree. Object-store request rates: nothing added scales with records, shards, partitions or indices; readChain is one GET per chain entry (a delta per segment) and the ancestry walk is per epoch, both on the allowed side of cost.md, and this is test-tier code besides.

findings.title: checkChain reports CLEAN for a chain it never read: absent epoch, empty chain, non-matching prefix
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED against the staged bytes with a throwaway probe: `Invariants.checkChain(new MemoryBinStore(), "bins/cluster-a", 7)` returns `[]`, and `Invariants.checkChain(new MemoryBinStore(), "no/such/prefix", 1)` returns `[]`. readChain LISTs, finds nothing, returns an empty list; inheritedOffsets returns immediately on `entries.isEmpty()`; the for-loop body never executes; the method returns an empty violation list. A caller cannot distinguish 'this chain is clean' from 'there was nothing here'. Concretely: M4.13's 1,000-seed sweep and M4.20's driver call this per epoch. If the driver's epoch range is off by one, or it passes the prefix the ingester writes rather than the one the sequencer writes, or a seed commits nothing at all (M4.20's row already records SEED 17 COMMITS ZERO AND REPORTS CLEAN), the sweep prints '0 violating seeds over N chains' having issued LISTs that returned nothing and zero GETs. That is the one thing the task says this class must never do. It is also the property the deleted crossEpochOffsetsChecked() flag nominally stood for -- the deletion is right (a hard-coded `return true` is not evidence) but nothing observable replaced it, so the class now has NO way to say how much it examined. No fixture pins any behaviour for an absent or empty chain, so the gap is unfalsified as well as unfixed. Remedy: either return a `chain`/`absent` Violation when the chain has no objects (or no CONTINUE at slot 0 and no entries), or return a result type carrying entriesExamined/chainsCrossed that the sweep can assert a floor on -- and give it a fixture asserting that an empty store is NOT reported clean.
findings.suggested_fix: Report an explicit violation for an empty chain, or return a record carrying counts of entries decoded and boundaries crossed, and pin it with a fixture.

findings.title: checkLink and the seal-bounded fold take the LAST Seal; the protocol's barrier is the FIRST, and checkChain's own I5 arm uses the first
findings.failure_scenario: Both loops are `for (ChainEntry e : prior) if (e instanceof Seal s) upTo = s.sequence();` and the same shape in checkLink, i.e. last-seal-wins. checkChain's I5 arm (lines 93-99) treats the FIRST seal as the barrier -- it fires for every entry after it -- so the file holds two different definitions of 'the seal'. MEASURED with a throwaway probe against the staged bytes: epoch 1 = Continue(0,0,0), delta(1) assigning 0..2, Seal(2, continuedAt=2), a fenced writer's delta(3) assigning 3..7, Seal(4, continuedAt=3); epoch 3 = Continue(0, prevEpoch=1, prevSeq=4), delta(1) resuming at 8. `checkChain(store, PREFIX, 3)` returns `[]`. The successor inherited the fenced writer's offsets, resumed 5 records above the real barrier at 3, and the checker called the boundary correct -- which is verbatim what offsetsBEYONDThePredecessorsSEALAreNOTInherited's own comment says must not happen ('would MASK the I2 violation that zombie caused, because the successor would appear to continue from it correctly'). That fixture passes only because its chain has exactly one Seal. This shape is reachable through production, not hypothetical: ChainReplay.chainEnd inspects only the LAST key of the chain (`last instanceof Seal s ? s : null`), so a chain whose highest slot is a post-seal delta yields seal==null, CommitLog.recoverChainEnd leaves sealedAt null, and CommitLog.seal's `if (sealedAt != null)` guard does not fire -- the next taker proposes at lastSeq+1 and wins a SECOND Seal past the barrier. Second measured case, same root cause: epoch 1 with Seal(2, continuedAt=2) then Seal(3, continuedAt=3), epoch 2 and epoch 3 both resuming the same stream at offset 3 -- a genuine fork handing the same offsets to different records. `checkChain(store, PREFIX, 3)` returns `[]`; the violation is reported against epoch 2, the legitimate successor, and the forker is the chain declared clean. Remedy: take the FIRST Seal in both places (and report a violation when a chain carries more than one), which also makes the file self-consistent with its own I5 arm.
findings.suggested_fix: Break on the first Seal encountered when computing upTo and closing, and report a violation for a second Seal in the same chain.

findings.title: The AB1 entry states 'recorded as M4.21' and M4.21 exists nowhere; it argues an already-landed task's round count, in this task's commit
findings.failure_scenario: `grep -rn 'M4\.21' docs scripts baselines` matches exactly one line: baselines/review.txt:11 itself. backlog.md has M4.12, M4.16, M4.17, M4.19, M4.20 and no M4.21. So the gap the entry says it recorded -- that check-reviewed.sh's round-cap path (the `ROUNDS > 2` branch, which calls `finish` before any baseline is consulted) never reads this file, which I confirmed by reading the script -- is NOT recorded anywhere actionable. A future reader greps M4.21, finds only the sentence that invented it, and the gap is lost. AGENTS.md names this exact defect ('And the ID must RESOLVE... An unresolvable ID is the same defect one step worse: it names nothing AND there is nothing to look up'), and the entry's own text confesses the same defect class three lines earlier ('three of them mine (a row that did not exist, ...)') -- it repeats the mistake it is describing. Compounding: (a) the entry argues M4.12's twelve-round count, and M4.12 already landed as 67606ab with this line absent from baselines/review.txt at HEAD, so by the file's own header ('An entry must be STAGED to count') it counted for nothing at the commit it argues, and staging it in M4.19 widens this commit past one-task-one-commit; (b) its own opening words are 'Round-count argument, not a finding argument', while the file's header says it holds 'Review findings argued as non-defects' -- so by its own admission it is the wrong file for it; (c) the key `AB1` is unqualified where the only precedent is `M0.31-R3-1`, and the header warns that an unqualified key silences another finding of the same number. Remedy: either add the M4.21 row (the check-reviewed.sh round-cap/baseline disconnect is a real, worthwhile row) or drop the claim, and move the round-count argument out of M4.19's commit.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the M4.21 backlog row the entry cites, or remove the claim; and keep the round-count argument out of M4.19's diff.

findings.title: The depth-1000 cap is the only termination argument, and the strictly-decreasing-epoch rule production calls corrupt is not checked
findings.failure_scenario: inheritedOffsets guards recursion with `depth > 1000` and silently returns an empty map. ChainReplay's own javadoc records that exact cap as measured-FALSE ('at 1002 legitimate terms every node's start threw... the cluster could never elect a sequencer again while being told its correct history was corrupt bytes') and replaced it with an iterative walk terminating on the epoch STRICTLY DECREASING -- a rule the checker does not restate anywhere. MEASURED: a chain whose CONTINUE names its own epoch (Continue(0, prevEpoch=5, 2) under epoch 5, Seal(2, continuedAt=5)) passes checkLink cleanly, recurses 1,000 levels re-reading the same chain twice per level (~2,000 LISTs and ~3,000 GETs against MemoryBinStore), and then reports a SPURIOUS `I2` ('resumes at 0 but the chain had assigned up to 3') rather than naming the corrupt link -- while production's replayAncestry throws IOException on the same bytes. So the checker tolerates a state production refuses to create, misattributes it, and pays a four-figure request count doing so. Beyond 1,000 legitimate terms the truncation silently under-inherits and turns every ancestor's history into spurious `gap` violations, which will read as real defects in M4.13's sweep. Remedy: report a `link` violation when `opening.prevEpoch() >= epoch`, and let that be the termination argument as it is in production.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a violation for a non-decreasing prevEpoch and drop the depth cap, mirroring ChainReplay's termination argument rather than the cap it removed.

findings.title: Half the Violation labels are not invariant IDs and the record carries no marker, so a consumer that filters on I-names drops the link arm
findings.failure_scenario: Violation is `(String invariant, String detail)` and the six values the class emits are I1, I2, I5, `chain`, `gap` and `link`. The class is named Invariants and its javadoc opens 'I1-I5 as predicates', which invites a consumer to write the natural filter -- `filteredOn(v -> v.invariant().startsWith("I"))`, or a switch over I1/I2/I5 to attribute a failing seed to an invariant. That filter silently discards `link`, which is the ONLY arm that catches either of the two defects this task was split out for (the successor's-word boundary and the disowned/omitted link), and `gap`, which is the half of the I2 split that this commit newly introduced. Nothing in the record or the javadoc's 'WHAT IS AND IS NOT CHECKED HERE' list says three of the labels are not invariant IDs. The I2/gap split itself is correct -- architecture.md:87 defines I2 as 'A committed offset is never reassigned', so only a rewind qualifies -- so the fix is to make the non-I labels impossible to filter away by accident (a severity/kind field, or an enum) rather than to re-merge them.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the label an enum or add a kind field so a consumer cannot silently select only the I-named arms.

findings.title: An EMPTY predecessor is walked past for offsets but simultaneously reported as an unsealed link -- two answers to one chain, on a shape production says it measured
findings.failure_scenario: Invariants.neverOpened treats an empty chain and a Seal-at-slot-0 chain identically ('A chain that carries no link'), and the walk-back steps past both. checkLink does not: for a Seal-at-0 predecessor it finds the seal and validates continuedAt/prevSeq (which is why offsetsAreINHERITEDAcrossAChainThatWasNeverOPENED is clean), but for a COMPLETELY empty predecessor `closing == null` and it reports `link: ... is NOT SEALED -- its writer met no barrier`. ChainReplay's javadoc names that shape as reachable and measured: 'A leader that acquires an epoch and dies before writing its CONTINUE leaves either a Seal at slot 0 ... or NOTHING AT ALL, if the successor died before that too... Measured: two consecutive takeovers each failing at or before their first PUT -- a store outage spanning a failover'. Since LocalSequencer.start always names prevEpoch = epoch - 1, the leader after that pair continues from an empty chain and the checker reports a link violation while its own offsets are correct. In M4.13's sweep that is a false positive on a fault the injector is built to produce, and the likely response to a false positive is a baselines entry that also suppresses the true positives of the same arm. Decide which it is and say so in one place: either an empty chain has no writer to fence and the arm should skip it (matching neverOpened), or an in-flight opening PUT can still land and an empty unsealed chain IS a hazard -- in which case the walk-back must not silently treat it as history-free.
findings.suggested_fix: Make checkLink and neverOpened agree on the empty-chain shape, and state which reading of the protocol was chosen.

findings.title: The javadoc's disclosure list presents I5 as covered when only one of its two clauses is, and the backlog row says the files are untracked while being the commit that tracks them
findings.failure_scenario: The javadoc block is explicitly framed as 'WHAT IS AND IS NOT CHECKED HERE, stated rather than implied', and it does the honest thing for I3/I4 ('NOT-RUN here'). It does not for I5: architecture.md:90 defines I5 as two clauses -- 'No acknowledged commit exists beyond a SEAL in its own chain' AND 'a commit is acked only after every lower-numbered write is confirmed (ADR-0011)' -- and only the structural first clause is checked. The ack-ordering clause is M4.11, which is `todo`, and whose row warns that today's serial CommitLog satisfies it BY ACCIDENT. So a reader of the disclosure list believes I5 is delivered and the sweep will report I5 clean while never having examined ack ordering at all. Second, smaller instance of the same class: the row this commit marks **done** still opens '⚠️ NEITHER IS TRACKED YET, so this row delivers the CLASS ... and a fresh clone has none of it', which is false the moment this commit lands -- the row describes the state before itself, which is the defect its own history says it was rewritten twice to stop doing.
findings.suggested_fix: Say in the javadoc that I5's ack-ordering clause is NOT-RUN and belongs to M4.11, and reword the row's tracking clause to the past tense.
